classification.difficultyReason: Infer two successive derivative graphs from stationary points, slope signs and changes in concavity, without numerical coordinates.

content.prompt: By considering the sign of the graph, sketch $f'(x)$ and then sketch $f''(x)$.

answer.short: An upward-opening parabola with two positive $x$-intercepts aligned with the stationary points of $f$. It is negative between them and positive outside.
answer.worked: The slopes of $f$ are positive, then negative, then positive. At both stationary points, $f'(x)=0$. Draw an upward-opening parabola crossing the axis directly beneath these points, with its vertex below the axis.

spec.description: Upward-opening parabola with both roots positive and its vertex below the axis.

answer.short: An increasing straight line crossing the $x$-axis directly beneath the vertex of $f'$, at a positive $x$-value.
answer.worked: The graph of $f'$ decreases to its minimum and then increases. Therefore $f''$ is negative before that minimum, zero at it and positive after it. Draw an increasing straight line with its zero aligned with the vertex of $f'$.

spec.description: Increasing straight line with a positive x-intercept aligned with the preceding parabola's vertex.
spec.mathematics: Schematic line with zero at the midpoint of the first-derivative roots; numerical coordinates are not givens.

answer.short: A downward-opening parabola crossing at the two stationary points of $f$, one negative and one positive. It is positive between them and negative outside.
answer.worked: The graph of $f$ decreases, then increases, then decreases, so $f'$ is negative, then positive, then negative. Its zeros align with the local minimum and maximum of $f$. Draw a downward-opening parabola with its vertex above the axis and slightly right of the $y$-axis.

answer.worked: The graph of $f'$ increases to its maximum and then decreases. Thus $f''$ is positive before the maximum, zero at it and negative after it. Draw a decreasing straight line whose zero aligns with the vertex of $f'$.
